articles.title: Muere Dolly Parton: la fabulosa vida de una de las estrellas más queridas en imágenes
articles.summary: La cantante estrella de la música country, que surgió de orígenes humildes, llegó a convertirse en una de las artistas más queridas del mundo.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, la superestrella de la música country originaria de las Grandes Montañas Humeantes de Tennessee, pasó de unos orígenes humildes a convertirse en una de las artistas más queridas del mundo.

Esta admiración global se reflejó este martes en la cantidad de mensajes y muestras de cariño que se produjeron tras conocerse la noticia de su muerte, a los 80 años.

A lo largo de una carrera que abarcó más de 60 años, vendió más de 100 millones de discos, escribió más de 3.000 canciones y ganó 11 premios Grammy, incluido un reconocimiento a la trayectoria artística.

Siempre se describió a sí misma, ante todo, como compositora. "Es mi forma de expresarme. Es mi terapia", dijo en una ocasión.

Dolly Rebecca Parton creció en la pobreza en una cabaña de una sola habitación a orillas del río Little Pigeon, en las montañas Smoky de Tennessee, siendo la cuarta de 12 hijos.

De niña, actuó en la radio y la televisión locales, y grabó su primer sencillo a los 13 años.

Tras mudarse a Nashville al día siguiente de graduarse en la escuela secundaria del condado de Sevier, Dolly Parton consiguió su primer éxito en solitario con Dumb Blonde en 1966.

En 1967, la estrella de la música country Porter Wagoner invitó a Parton a unirse a The Porter Wagoner Show , dándole un papel fijo en su programa de televisión de distribución nacional, así como un lugar en su espectáculo teatral itinerante.

Su gran éxito llegó con el álbum Hello, I'm Dolly .

El 4 de enero de 1969 se convirtió en miembro del Grand Ole Opry , el programa radiofónico de música country más antiguo de Estados Unidos.

Parton lo describió como la "iglesia de mi corazón" y dijo que participar en él era un sueño de toda la vida.

En una memorable sesión de composición en 1973, Parton escribió dos de sus mayores éxitos: Jolene y I Will Always Love You .

Tras haber escrito miles de canciones a lo largo de su dilatada carrera, Parton afirmó que componer canciones era su mayor forma de autoexpresión.

Conocida por su imagen extravagante y deslumbrante, Dolly Parton combinó lentejuelas, ingenio y encanto para mantener una carrera que abarcó desde la música country hasta el pop comercial.

Fue cabeza de cartel en festivales y se convirtió en una estrella mundial con álbumes como Here You Come Again .

Parton también se hizo famosa por colaboraciones memorables, en particular con Kenny Rogers, cuyo dúo Islands in the Stream se convirtió en uno de los éxitos más representativos de la década de 1980.

Si bien Dolly Parton es más conocida por su extensa carrera musical, su trabajo como actriz también ha dejado una huella imborrable en el público cinematográfico.

El papel que lanzó a la fama a Parton en la pantalla grande llegó en la comedia de oficina de 1980 9 to 5 , donde compartió cartel con Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin y Dabney Coleman.

Su interpretación de Doralee Rhodes combinó un gran sentido del humor con calidez, lo que ayudó a redefinir las expectativas sobre los artistas que dan el salto de la música al cine.

Posteriormente participó en películas como The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas , junto a Burt Reynolds, y Steel Magnolias ("Magnolias de acero").

Esta última cuenta con un reparto monumental que incluye a Julia Roberts y Sally Field junto a Shirley MacLaine, Olympia Dukakis y Daryl Hannah.

En estas interpretaciones, Parton demostró un equilibrio entre humor y profundidad emocional, a menudo dotando a las escenas de una presencia discreta y marcada.

En 1986, Dolly Parton inauguró Dollywood, un parque temático en Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, cerca de su lugar de nacimiento.

Se convirtió en una importante atracción turística, uno de los parques temáticos regionales más visitados de EE.UU..

El éxito del parque ayudó a financiar la fundación benéfica de Parton y su programa de alfabetización.

A través de su Biblioteca de la Imaginación, fundada en honor a su padre, que no sabía leer, Dolly Parton regaló más de 100 millones de libros a niños de todo el mundo.

Su propio libro, Coat of Many Colours , fue el libro número 100 millones que ese programa donó a la colección de la Biblioteca del Congreso de Estados Unidos.

Un ayuntamiento de Escocia anunció que dedicaría un día al año a Dolly Parton para conmemorar el impacto de su programa de fomento de la lectura.

Parton donó personalmente millones a la investigación médica y al socorro en casos de desastre.

La cantante también lideró varias iniciativas importantes de ayuda en casos de desastre, entre las que destaca la creación de My People Fund tras los incendios forestales de las Grandes Montañas Humeantes de 2016, que distribuyó unos US$10 millones a las familias que perdieron sus hogares.

Reunió a un elenco estelar de artistas para un teletón de tres horas con el fin de recaudar fondos.

En 2024, prometió US$2 millones para ayudar a los damnificados por el huracán Helene en el este de Tennessee y los Apalaches, combinando una donación personal con el apoyo equivalente de sus empresas y su fundación.

La actuación de Parton en el Festival de Glastonbury de 2014 se convirtió rápidamente en una de las actuaciones más emblemáticas en la sección de "Leyendas" de la historia del evento.

Con una de las mayores afluencias diurnas que ha tenido el festival, estimada en más de 180.000 personas, convirtió el escenario Pyramid en un coro multitudinario, con interpretaciones de Jolene , 9 to 5 y I Will Always Love You que provocaron escenas de participación casi unánime del público.

En 2019, Parton celebró sus 50 años como miembro del Opry con un importante programa especial de televisión titulado Dolly Parton: 50 Years at the Opry .

El evento incluyó actuaciones y homenajes de otros artistas de música country.

Su relación de décadas con el Opry ayudó a consolidar su estatus como guardián de la tradición de la música country y como escenario para las estrellas modernas.

Parton comenzó a alejarse gradualmente de las grandes giras, diciendo que ya no quería pasar largos periodos de tiempo en la carretera.

En cambio, se centró en conciertos selectos, nuevos proyectos discográficos y apariciones en pantalla, incluyendo Dolly Parton's Heartstrings , Mountain Magic y Christmas on the Square para Netflix .

En 2021, Parton recibió públicamente la vacuna contra la covid-19 en el Centro Médico de la Universidad de Vanderbilt, aprovechando la ocasión para animar a otros a hacer lo mismo.

Interpretó una versión adaptada de su éxito Jolene , cantando: "Vacuna, vacuna, vacuna, vacuna, te lo ruego, por favor no lo dudes".

La incorporación de Parton al Salón de la Fama del Rock and Roll en 2022 marcó un giro de autoconciencia muy característico de ella.

Tras haber dicho inicialmente que no se había "ganado" el honor, más tarde lo aceptó con humor, declarando "ahora soy una estrella del rock", antes de interpretar su nueva canción Rockin' , escrita especialmente para la ceremonia, un paso simbólico hacia su posterior álbum de rock Rockstar.

En 2023, Parton protagonizó otro momento memorable en directo cuando actuó en el espectáculo del medio tiempo del partido de Acción de Gracias de los Dallas Cowboys, luciendo un traje de animadora del equipo adornado con pedrería.

Más recientemente, Parton continuó compaginando las pérdidas personales con nuevos proyectos creativos.

Después del fallecimiento de su marido, Carl Dean, en 2025, lanzó If You Hadn't Been There en su homenaje, al tiempo que continuaba con el desarrollo de Dolly: A True Original Musical , la producción teatral basada en su vida y carrera.

A principios de 2026, Parton pronunció un discurso de homenaje pregrabado para Ozzy Osbourne en los premios BRIT en Manchester, donde Ozzy recibió un premio póstumo a la trayectoria artística.

Su discurso fue breve, pero constituyó uno de los momentos más emotivos de la ceremonia.

Parton tenía previsto regresar a los escenarios para una breve temporada en Las Vegas, pero este mes anunció que cancelaba la serie de conciertos debido a problemas de salud, y les dijo a sus fans que necesitaba "un poco más de tiempo para recuperarse".

Ella seguirá siendo un ícono cultural recordado por su generosidad y humor, así como por su extraordinaria capacidad para componer canciones, el arte que constituye la base de un catálogo que ha dado forma a la música country moderna y ha trascendido generaciones.

articles.title: Female Virginia officer sues police department after allegedly sharing locker room with biological male
articles.summary: Former Norfolk police officer Meghan Grabow sued her police department earlier this month after sharing a women's changing room with a biological male in 202...
articles.body:
A former Norfolk, Virginia , police officer filed a lawsuit against the city and its police chief earlier this month after the police department allegedly allowed a biological male to use the women's locker rooms.

According to the documents obtained by Fox News Digital , the Aug. 10 legal complaint stemmed from an August 2024 incident in which former Norfolk police officer Meghan Grabow was changing in the women's locker room and stripped down to her underwear when a recruit described as a "biological male who identifies as a woman" entered the room wearing a suit and tie. Grabow said that the recruit looked at her "as a man would look at a woman" before moving to another part of the locker room.

Grabow claimed that when she spoke to her superiors about her discomfort, she was told to "learn to deal with it" and "find another locker room" if she was uncomfortable.

San Francisco Ymca Changes Locker Room Rules After Transgender Controversy: Report

In addition to this incident, Grabow said that she and other concerned officers were told by police chief Mark Talbot that the "woman" hired by the department "will use the restroom that's appropriate for her gender" and were repeatedly instructed to refer to the recruit as "she."

Other officers also voiced concerns that they were not warned about sharing facilities with a biological male , something Talbot acknowledged could have been handled "better."

Appeals Court Revives Lawsuit By Alaska Airlines Flight Attendants Fired After Opposing Pride Message

Grabow later received an indefinite suspension pending termination in 2025 over a minor traffic violation committed prior to the incident after attempting to voice a complaint. Other officers have since left the department over their backlash to the transgender policy, the complaint states.

Grabow is seeking $15 million in compensatory damages, claiming Talbot and the police department were guilty of intentional infliction of emotional distress as well as violating her religious freedoms by forcing her to share a changing facility with a biological male and validate transgender ideology against her Catholic beliefs .

Christian Lifeguard Who Refused Pride Flag Duties And Was Suspended Is Now Headed Toward Trial

Attorney Scott Lloyd, who is representing Grabow in the case, told Fox News Digital in a statement that they are determined to protect female-only spaces through this case.

"We need to defend private spaces for the women who rely on them. Officer Grabow has done a brave and admirable thing by stepping forward, but it shouldn't have come to this," Lloyd said.

The Norfolk Police Department declined to comment to Fox News Digital, saying that it "cannot comment on pending litigation or personnel-related matters."

Under 2020 guidelines for the Norfolk Police Department, employees are encouraged not to question a transgender person's identity except for "articulable reasons," such as if they are related to a crime.

"Employees will respect an individual's gender identity and gender expression. An individual's gender expression may be traits that are not typically associated with a person's assigned sex at birth; these expressions may include wigs, prosthetics, makeup, adopted name, tone of voice, clothing, mannerisms, etc.," the 2020 general order read.

articles.title: What has happened in Plaid Cymru's's first 100 days in Welsh government?
articles.summary: Plaid ministers say they are making good progress but the opposition say little has been achieved.
articles.body:
Plaid Cymru claimed victory in celebratory scenes on the steps of the Senedd in May, after it inflicted a heavy and historic defeat on Welsh Labour.

Since then, it has been an occasionally rough ride for Rhun ap Iorwerth's minority administration.

After 100 days in charge, Plaid ministers say they have laid the foundations to improve public services, and have already made a "tangible" impact in areas like childcare.

But the government failed to get over its first significant hurdle in the Senedd, when its supplementary budget was rejected by the entire Senedd opposition.

Meanwhile opposition parties claim little has changed since Plaid took charge.

Plaid Cymru formed the first non-Labour Welsh government in May, with the party six seats short of a majority of 49.

It won the election on a platform of challenging Westminster to give Wales more control over its own affairs, a promise of a major programme to boost childcare, and to cut waiting times.

The party set out a plan for the first 100 days ahead of the election, which it said showed how serious it was about governing.

It was criticised at the time as a "plan to have a plan", with the party promising to commission a number of reviews or strategies.

The Welsh government said it had made progress on a number of issues in its first few months, including extending free school meals to more secondary school pupils, a new north-south coach service, and a multi-year funding deal for farmers.

But there's a been a focus on a few big areas over the last few months.

Early on, Plaid came under pressure to spell out how it would deliver its landmark childcare policy, which would see free care expanded over a four-year period.

Currently parents in work or training can get up to 30 hours a week for children aged three or four. Plaid want to expand this so at least 20 hours is available from nine months to four years old.

Opposition parties have repeatedly pressured Plaid ministers for answers as to how this will work, demanding costings and a timetable for how the expanded scheme will work - leading a minister to promise more detail .

There were questions from councils , who said the proposal faced serious challenges because of a lack of resources and staff.

The Welsh government now says that all local authorities are on track to provide 12.5 hours of free child-care to two-year-olds via the Flying Start scheme by next March.

Plaid ministers want to phase the rest of the scheme over time - but until that is spelled out the party will continue to face scrutiny over how it's achieved.

The length of time that patients have to wait in the NHS was a totemic problem faced by the previous Welsh Labour government.

Plaid Cymru was careful not to raise expectation of an immediate improvement, telling the BBC last February that the public would not expect a difference within the first 100 days .

The party promised to get waiting times "down to pre-pandemic levels" within four years. In June, the Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor said he would eradicate two-year waits in a matter of months .

The latest figures saw two-year waits drop slightly - by 3% to just under 4,100 pathways - but for the third month in a row the total numbers waiting for treatment has risen.

Government Efficiency Minister Dafydd Trystan Davies said the government was laying "the foundations for success to bring down waiting lists" - pointing to work on surgical hubs and a workforce plan.

Plaid is in a minority in the Senedd and the party is vulnerable to defeats if the opposition votes against it.

That happened a few times before the summer recess, including in a crucial vote on an extra Â£300m in spending to reduce NHS waits and expand childcare.

Labour had demanded Â£100m extra to be spent on children with additional learning needs - and the two sides had failed to come to an agreement.

It was the first time a Welsh government has lost a vote on a supplementary budget - which is in addition to the main budget exercise that happens in the autumn.

Laura McAllister, professor of politics at Cardiff University, said she thought the government had been a little naive.

"If you're in that position of being a minority government, transactional relationships and goodwill between the parties is absolutely fundamental."

Since then, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has indicated that he does want a budget deal with Plaid .

The Plaid government faced its first major incident over the summer as a devolved government when a number of wildfires broke out in Wales.

The Welsh government came under scrutiny for its crisis management, because unlike the police, fire services are devolved in Wales.

There was criticism from Reform Wales about the time taken in to bring in the army and aerial support .

A minister said lessons needed to be learned with wildfires more likely in the future due to climate change.

Plaid Cymru wants powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure and the Crown Estate to be devolved from Westminster to Cardiff.

It promised negotiations with Westminster to do that, but turmoil in London has made making the case tricky.

Ap Iorwerth tried and failed to get a meeting with the previous prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, although the man now in charge, Andy Burnham, held his first face-to-face meeting with the first minister in July .

Burnham has promised to put devolution front and centre of his government.

But his Welsh Secretary, Stephen Kinnock, has said he is not yet "entirely convinced" by the case for more responsibilities for the Welsh government.

Some at Collier's Adventure Farm in Nelson, Caerphilly, were willing to give the Plaid Cymru government time before rushing to judgement.

Raydean Thomas said: "I think they're finding their feet at the moment. Nothing that they've done has been wrong as far as I can say. I think they're thinking of things in the right way."

Faye Dalgleish-McGee said: "People do rush to have an opinion a bit too quickly - let them get settled in before we start complaining."

Meanwhile, Trish Garner said it was important to wait to see what their plans are.

"But I don't hear an awful lot about what they're going to do and that's my feeling," she added.

Michael Davies said his life had not changed since Plaid had got into power, and that politics was the "same old story" with successive governments blaming each other.

"[They say] it's going to take us x amount of years to put it right and then nothing seems to happen."

Julie Jones, who was also at the coffee morning, said it was too soon to judge ap Iorwerth, but that "he came in all guns blazing".

Dafydd Trystan Davies said that "the initial work has been completed on the 96 actions" in the party's 100-day plan.

He said that in some areas the administration had "put the foundations for success in place".

"But in others, we've made tangible real progress that people will be able to feel already," he said.

The first minister is on leave until the end of the week and was unavailable for interviews ahead of the completion of 100 days in government.

Asked by BBC Wales whether that meant the government was playing down the milestone, Davies said it was him that was responsible for 100-day programme and that ap Iorwerth will issue a "progress report" next week.

Reform accused Plaid of focusing too much on "reviews, committees and plans".

Dan Thomas, Reform's Welsh leader, told BBC Wales that things have "just got worse" since Plaid won the election, with waiting lists having "gone up".

"The first minister said during the election campaign that two-year waits would be eradicated within a matter of months. We're now three months into a Plaid government and we're nowhere near seeing those waits being eradicated."

Ken Skates, leader of Welsh Labour, said there was "quite a contrast" between Plaid Cymru's first 100 days and the start of Andy Burnham's premiership.

"We've seen plans and processes here, discussion, a lot of talk, very little action. In contrast with Andy Burnham, we've seen some really, really big interventions that are going to make a difference to people's lives."

Darren Millar MS, Leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd, said: "Plaid's first 100 days have been a disappointing series of missed opportunities to turn the page on 27 years of Labour rule in Wales."

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's Last Words to Her 3 Kids Before Their Deaths Revealed
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy’s last words to her and husband Patrick Clancy's three kids before their 2023 deaths were revealed as Dr. Kirk Heilbrun testified in the trial...
articles.body:
Content warning: This story discusses violence against children and suicidal ideation.

New details are coming to light in the Lindsay Clancy case.

During court proceedings for the 36-year-old—who is on trial for three counts of first-degree murder after admitting to killing her and then-husband Patrick Clancy 's kids Cora , 5, Dawson , 3 and Callan , 8 months, in 2023—forensic psychologist Dr. Kirk Heilbrun revealed the last words that the former labor and delivery nurse told her children before strangling them and trying to kill herself.

During his testimony Aug. 24, which was livestreamed by Associated Press , Heilbrun—who evaluated Lindsay for three days in April—testified that she killed her children as part of what he described as "altruistic filicide," saying she believed they would suffer without her and that killing them would allow them to be "together in heaven."

As she killed them, she told the children, according to Heilbrun, "Go to God, baby. Go to God."

The psychologist also revealed what Lindsay said to Patrick after he returned home and asked what she had done. According to Heilbrun, she replied, "I tried to kill myself."

Dolly Parton, Country Music Legend, Dead at 80

Dolly Parton Shared How She Wanted to Be Remembered Before Death

Lindsay admitted to strangling her three children to death using an exercise band in January 2023 before attempting to take her own life by jumping out of a second-story window. She suffered a fall that left her paralyzed from the waist down.

While she has not denied killing her three kids, Lindsay has pleaded not guilty for criminal responsibility in their murders due to her state of mind during the incident, which her defense attorney Kevin Reddington is arguing was compromised due to postpartum psychosis.

Heilbrun said Lindsay's response to Patrick was inconsistent with psychosis, noting that someone experiencing hallucinations likely would have replied differently.

However, he also noted that Lindsay shared with him that she did hear a male voice about 18 minutes before the murders, which said, "Kill the kids so you can kill yourself."

"The way she described this as happening is that she heard a voice that she'd never heard before, experienced a hallucination and she's never experienced it since. But she only experienced it for the 18 minutes or so that it took to kill the children," Heilbrun testified. "To put it mildly, that would be a very, very unusual pattern or manifestation of how this kind of thing comes about. Very unusual."

Heilbrun told the court he diagnosed Lindsay with Bipolar II disorder. Saying she experienced both manic and depressive episodes, he admitted the diagnosis was difficult to reach "because of all the diagnoses in the records and all the symptoms that she experienced."

Heilbrun also brought up Lindsay's Catholic faith, which prompted Reddington to request a mistrial. Judge William Sullivan denied the motion.

Lindsay Clancy 's now-ex-husband was the first witness called to testify during her murder trial, which began July 27 in Plymouth Superior Court. The 35-year-old former nurse has not denied killing daughter Cora , 5, and sons Dawson , 3, and Callan , 8 months, but has pleaded not guilty of murder, the defense attributing her actions to postpartum psychosis. Patrick Clancy testified that Lindsay struggled with her mental health after giving birth to Callan in May 2023, according to CNN . She also sought treatment after Dawson was born in 2019, he said, "but it didn't last very long." Lindsay's "big spiral," as he referred to it, occurred in December 2023 after she started taking a new medication, one of several she'd been prescribed since September, Patrick said. He testified that Lindsay told him she had "intrusive thoughts" about harming their children and herself. He didn't worry about the kids' safety, he said, because she didn't seem to have "any intention" of actually hurting them. On Dec. 31, Patrick said, Lindsay went to the E.R. at Massachusetts General Hospital "because she was still talking about thoughts of suicide . She was admitted to an affiliated psychiatric facility, and when she was discharged Jan. 5 she seemed "much better."

On Jan. 24, 2023, Lindsay "was having one of her best days," Patrick testified, per CNN , recalling that his then-wife built a snowman in the yard. "She was playing with the kids," he said, "and she seemed in a good mood." That morning she had taken Cora to a doctor's appointment and he had texted her a picture of Dawson after he "dressed himself completely for the first time." Patrick told the court he had felt "hopeful" since his wife's release from the hospital. "Her mood seemed better," he said. "She was more active, and she was able...to partake in more things." Before he left to pick up dinner and medication for Cora, he said he kissed one of the kids on the head and told them he'd "be right back." Prosecutors allege Lindsay sent Patrick on errands to get him out of the house on purpose. Then, Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham said in her opening statement, she strangled the children with exercise bands "deliberately and meticulously." Patrick testified July 29 that no one told him he shouldn't leave Linday alone with their kids, telling the court, "I didn't know what psychosis was until after this happened."

In the audio recording of Patrick's seven-minute 911 call that was played in court July 29, according to the Associated Press , he's heard telling the dispatcher, who repeatedly asks what happened, "She killed the kids!"

Lindsay wrote about her struggles, including that she felt "incredibly sad and guilty" about not breastfeeding Callan, according to journal excerpts read to jurors Aug. 5. "I want help," she wrote in an entry read by her attorney. "I want to be well." In another, she said, "I have crazy brain fog. I feel like I can't make a plan. I live moment to moment waiting for the next nap time. I'm terrified of Cal getting overtired now because I feel can't help him."

It marked the close of several demanding years in which studying had to fit around a large family, foster care and a sudden change in the way she experienced the world.As reported by People, Porter received her masterâs degree from Grand Canyon University on April 29, 2026, walking across the commencement stage in a purple gown. Her diagnosis came during the COVID-19 pandemic, a period when Porter was already dealing with the uncertainty of her changing hearing.The effect was not limited to classrooms or conversations. Porter experienced pain and other problems, and medical examinations showed that the device was failing. She was eventually told that electricity was leaking from the implant into her head. She was raising a family of 11 children while completing her degree, including children who had joined the family through foster care and adoption.Her experience with foster care began when she and her then-husband took in a child and later decided to foster that child's three older siblings as well. Porter was 25 at the time.She later recalled that she did not want the siblings to be separated from one another, so the family took all four children in. Porter ultimately gave birth to six of her children. Her youngest, the 11th, was adopted while she was already in graduate school.That meant coursework and family responsibilities were running side by side. There were days when the demands of the degree felt difficult to manage, Porter acknowledged, and she has spoken about the tears that came during the programme. articles.title: Brazil fines TikTok $30m for child data privacy violations
articles.summary: Owner ByteDance ordered to erase illegally obtained child data in Brazil as crackdown on tech giants intensifies.
articles.body:
Brazil's data protection authority has fined TikTok's parent company, ByteDance, nearly $30m for the alleged mishandling of children and teenagers' personal data, in the nation's latest move against social media companies.

The regulatory body said in its ruling that TikTok had breached data privacy laws across both logged-in accounts and guest browsing sessions by collecting and processing young users' personal information without a valid legal basis or adequate safeguards.

The regulator estimated that TikTok may have processed the data of at least 8 million children, highlighting what they said were systemic deficiencies within the platform's age-verification mechanism.

The company can still appeal the decision in the next 10 days, according to the regulator.

The ruling also includes an order for TikTok to erase all data amassed illegally.

Brazil's regulatory authority also mandated the company to formulate an improved comprehensive youth-protection framework, stressing that TikTok's "logged-out feed", which allows users to browse content without creating an account, enables widespread use ‌of the ⁠platform by minors while bypassing age-verification checks.

According to the regulator, the feature is available in Brazil but not in the United States or Europe, where access is solely restricted to registered users.

Earlier this month, the regulator ordered the social media platform Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature across the country, accusing the platform of failing to protect children and teenagers. The move came after a 13-year-old girl died by suicide following a livestream in which authorities say she was encouraged to harm herself.

The voice and text chat app, hugely popular with gamers, launched in 2015.

Brazil's government, under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the Supreme Court have tried to regulate internet use by minors, with mixed results so far, at a moment when countries such as Australia, Canada and Indonesia are undertaking similar efforts.

articles.title: Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder of Stacy Hunter
articles.summary: An online petition calls for greater use of technology to protect women from abusive partners following the killing of Stacy Hunter in Renfrewshire.
articles.body:
Domestic abuse campaigners are calling for greater use of location tracking technology to monitor high-risk suspects following the murder of a woman in Renfrewshire last month.

An online petition is calling for a "Stacy's law" in memory of Stacy Hunter who was killed at her home near Houston by her estranged husband while he was on bail.

Scottish ministers have previously faced criticism over the slow rollout of Global Positioning System (GPS) equipment, which is used far less in Scotland than in some other countries.

The Scottish government said it was listening to victims and support organisations and would carefully consider the petition.

Woman found dead was murdered, police say, as man's death still 'unexplained'

Man found dead with murdered wife had been accused of attacking her

The campaign has been started by Lynne Mackenzie, herself a domestic abuse survivor, who lives a few miles from the isolated cottage where Stacy was killed in July.

Stacy's husband Jim Mair, 43, whose body was found beside her, had been charged with assaulting her but had reportedly been granted bail on condition that he did not approach her.

While Mackenzie did not know Stacy personally, she said she was shocked at her murder which happened just six days after the death of another domestic abuse victim, Vikki Soloman, in Edinburgh.

She told BBC Scotland News the killings led her to question whether enough was being done to protect women in Stacy's situation.

"Every time driving in and out of the village I was aware of the police at the end of the road," she said.

"And it really got me thinking what could we have done? What could have been put in place beforehand? What else do we need?"

She has been in contact with Stacy's family who have agreed for her name to be associated with the campaign.

The petition calls for high-risk domestic abuse perpetrators or suspects released on bail to have their location monitored using GPS equipment.

This could include individually assessed exclusion zones around victim's homes or workplaces and alerts that trigger police responses when conditions are breached.

Mike Nellis, emeritus professor of criminal and community justice at the University of Strathclyde and one of the UK's leading experts on electronic monitoring, said it was perfectly feasible to introduce such a system.

He said it could work by setting an exclusion zone around a victim's home that triggered an alert if an abuser violated it, although the zone would have to be sufficiently large to allow time for police to get there first.

Prof Nellis said that while Scotland has been slow to embrace GPS technology, the campaign could now find itself "pushing at an open door" because ministers are actively exploring ways of reducing the prison population.

However, he cautioned that no system was foolproof.

"I think probably every jurisdiction that has used it has at one point in time had an offender who still managed to assault, injure or kill the victim," he told BBC Scotland News.

"It's a helpful solution but it's not perfect."

He also added that some women's support groups have in the past voiced concern that such systems might give a false sense of security.

In Scotland, electronic tagging has mainly relied on older radio frequency (RF) equipment which is focused on home curfews or detention.

These devices are linked to a receiver in the offender's home and cannot track movements away from the property.

Last year, the independent public body Community Justice Scotland (CJS) issued an urgent National Improvement Recommendation to the Scottish government urging it to accelerate the expansion of more sophisticated monitoring systems.

CJS expressed frustration that neither GPS nor alcohol monitoring technologies had been adopted in Scotland despite an expert group having backed them in 2016.

By contrast, both technologies have already been widely used in England and Wales since 2018 and there are plans to start imposing new restriction zones on offenders this autumn.

Scotland's victims minister, Kirsten Oswald, said her thoughts were with Stacy's family.

In a statement she said: "We are listening carefully to victims and support organisations about what more can be done to prevent and tackle violence against women and girls and we will carefully consider the petition.

"The first minister has pledged his personal leadership on tackling the scourge of violence against women and girls.

"As the first minister has made clear, government has a vital role to play in tackling violence against women and girls, but lasting change requires all of us to play our part."

She added: "Men, in particular, must challenge sexism, confront abusive behaviour and help create a culture where every woman and girl can live free from violence, abuse and fear.

"While decisions on bail and remand are always a matter for the independent court, bail can be electronically monitored."

Lynne Mackenzie is a co-founder of Rise Against Abuse , a not-for-profit group which supports those affected by domestic abuse, but she has started the petition in an individual capacity.

Stacy's family now prefer her to be remembered by her pre-marriage surname Hunter, rather than her husband's name Mair.

articles.title: Does 'rewilded' land need better wildfire prevention measures?
articles.summary: RSPB is considering measures it can take to improve resilience in the wake of a five week long fire
articles.body:
As we're driving in a pickup truck to see the aftermath of a huge fire which burnt for more than a month in the Cairngorms, I spot fresh smoke coming from the ground.

My guide - RSPB Scotland's site manager at the Abernethy nature reserve, Ben Oliver-Jones - puts the vehicle in reverse and we jump out to see what's happening.

It's one of several hot-spots which keeps emerging a full week after firefighters left the scene , which Ben likens to a game of whack-a-mole in an already charred landscape where the smell of burning still hangs heavily in the air.

But while the small pockets of smouldering vegetation are still being dealt with, attention is turning to improving wildfire protection.

More than 2,500 hectares of moorland and forest - about 10 square miles - was destroyed in the fire, which led to the evacuation of an entire village and where the smoke could be seen and smelt 60 miles (96.5km) away in Aberdeen.

Like a growing number of Scotland's estates, the Loch Garten and Abernethy nature reserve is being managed for ecological restoration - what others might describe as 'rewilding', a now polarising term which the RSPB avoids using.

Opponents have argued that the process leaves areas more vulnerable to uncontrollable fires, which the charity disputes, but it has identified significant land management changes it plans to make.

The changes focus on four key areas: fire breaks, wetlands, heather management and tree planting.

While the estate's network of tracks functioned as a fire break in some locations, in other areas strong winds helped high flames jump the gap.

Experts say fire from burning heather can reach heights of six metres and that fire breaks need to be three times the flame height.

RSPB Scotland says it now acknowledges that fire breaks need to be wider and has already started that process on its long network of forest trails.

Machines have been used to remove vegetation on either side of the track with the hope that what remains would not create such high flames if it were to ignite.

While it might look desolate now, the hope is that some insects and plant species will eventually colonise the ground either sides of the tracks.

It also plans to create more ponds and wet areas around the site which can be used as a source of water to pump onto fires.

A small fire on the reserve in June was extinguished using water from a pond created with cash from the Scottish government's nature restoration fund as a habitat for species like rare dragonflies.

The charity says it's working to raise water tables where bogs have been drained and create new areas of standing water for fire fighting.

Peatlands have proved problematic for wildfires because the fire can spread through the peat, deep underground as well as on the surface.

It's a problem for degraded peatland which makes up about 80% of Scotland's total, but for those in a near-natural state the peat can act as a defence.

In good condition, they keep the water level high, bringing moisture to the landscape.

Its effectiveness was demonstrated during a large fire near Melvich, Sutherland, in 2019 which reached an area that had been re-wetted 20 years earlier.

Roxane Anderson from the University of the Highlands and Islands (UNI) studied the land before and after the fire and says any damage to wet peatland was superficial and on the surface.

She argues that's a reason for accelerating peatland restoration which is currently targeting 400,000 hectares - about 1,500 square miles - by 2040 and describes it as "a complete no brainer."

"We should do it as much as we can, as quickly as we can and as strategically as we can, especially in the context of this changing climate."

On Monday, Scotland's chief fire officer published an open letter calling for better wildlife planning and urging a "more formal and proportionate fire safety regime" to match that for businesses in urban settings.

It comes as the Scottish government enters the final stages of introducing licences for muirburn - the controlled burning of heather on moorland primarily managed for grouse shooting.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.

RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.

It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.

While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.

The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."

Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.

The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.

It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.

Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.

But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.

Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.

He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.

He believes there is no silver bullet which will prevent a wildfire starting or spreading but that estates "need to build up layers of defence".

Firms affected by Cairngorms wildfire offered support from £3m fund

'Apocalyptic' damage as Cairngorms wildfire burns for two weeks

In April, the Cairngorms National Park Authority introduced a bylaw making it illegal to start a fire or a BBQ during the summer months to prevent wildfires.

Despite the huge blaze, figures suggest that move has been effective at reducing potential sources of ignition, with the number of campfires or barbecues recorded so far this year totalling 36 compared with 94 in the same period last year.

That's still too many but the reduction perhaps emphasises the importance of preventing a fire's spread.

Wildfires have been described to me as an "intermittent problem" because they're seasonal and we don't see large ones happening every year.

If they happened every year, it would become an obvious priority.

Preventing and tackling them both cost money and there are obvious questions around striking the balance between spending on both, not to mention wider affordability.

But climate change is predicted to bring more long, dry spells which create the tinderbox of summer 2026 and so all of this may be seen as an investment in the future.

For five weeks, land managers with very opposing views on how the uplands should be managed stood side by side battling the enormous blaze which was sweeping through the Cairngorms.

They found a common purpose and it's hoped that now seeing the countryside through a prism of wildfire risk may now be the unifier which sees them exchanging at least some practices - even if their end goals for the landscape still differ wildly.

Its effectiveness was demonstrated during a large fire near Melvich, Sutherland, in 2019 which reached an area that had been re-wetted 20 years earlier.

Roxane Anderson from the University of the Highlands and Islands (UNI) studied the land before and after the fire and says any damage to wet peatland was superficial and on the surface.

She argues that's a reason for accelerating peatland restoration which is currently targeting 400,000 hectares - about 1,500 square miles - by 2040 and describes it as "a complete no brainer."

"We should do it as much as we can, as quickly as we can and as strategically as we can, especially in the context of this changing climate."

On Monday, Scotland's chief fire officer published an open letter calling for better wildlife planning and urging a "more formal and proportionate fire safety regime" to match that for businesses in urban settings.

It comes as the Scottish government enters the final stages of introducing licences for muirburn - the controlled burning of heather on moorland primarily managed for grouse shooting.

Ministers have brought in the licences to make moorland more "environmentally sustainable", but Scottish Land and Estates say the practice is a valuable tool for reducing vegetation which can act as fuel to a wildfire.

RSPB Scotland does not practice muirburn but accepts that the "fuel load" does need to be managed.

It has been doing that through grazing cattle, which eat the vegetation, while in other areas land managers have used machines to cut and mulch the grass, gorse, bracken and heather.

While some sporting estates remain opposed to "rewilding", others have embraced some of the elements of ecological restoration.

The Rottal estate in the Angus Glens has been working with the RSPB for several years now and owner Dee Ward believes there is a lot of common ground.

He has been re-wetting peatland, planting trees and encouraging wading birds and says that while the "ideological extremists" have been holding the narrative, a lot more estates are trying to find the middle ground.

He added: "There are people that are very anti-grouse shooting. Fair enough, that's your choice. But that's clouding their view about muirburn because they're saying because grouse shooters do it, it must be bad."

Dee urges both sides to begin looking at land management practices through the lens of preventing wildfires and consider sharing appropriate methods.

The fourth move RSPB Scotland plans is the introduction of more broadleaved trees in its woodlands.

It says that while pines contain flammable resins, species such as alder, rowan, aspen and birch are higher in moisture content which means they do not burn as easily.

Abernethy hosts the largest and most important remnant of Scotland's ancient Caledonian pine forest and so the Scots pines are an important part of the mix.

But the charity wants to explore the option of increasing the proportion of other species, which would have occurred naturally in the original forest anyway.

Michael Bruce, owner of the Glen Tannar estate in Aberdeenshire, specialises in controlled burning of moorland and helps the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service with its wildfire forecasting.

He says that there hasn't been enough academic research and modelling in the UK on how wildfires behave to make land management changes meaningful.

While two significant studies have been carried out in Scotland over the past 25 years, neither has been long-term or consistent and he believes events of the summer demonstrate the need for improved understanding.

He believes there is no silver bullet which will prevent a wildfire starting or spreading but that estates "need to build up layers of defence".

Firms affected by Cairngorms wildfire offered support from Â£3m fund Published 6 August

Firms affected by Cairngorms wildfire offered support from Â£3m fund

'Apocalyptic' damage as Cairngorms wildfire burns for two weeks Published 29 July

'Apocalyptic' damage as Cairngorms wildfire burns for two weeks

In April, the Cairngorms National Park Authority introduced a bylaw making it illegal to start a fire or a BBQ during the summer months to prevent wildfires.

Despite the huge blaze, figures suggest that move has been effective at reducing potential sources of ignition, with the number of campfires or barbecues recorded so far this year totalling 36 compared with 94 in the same period last year.

That's still too many but the reduction perhaps emphasises the importance of preventing a fire's spread.

Wildfires have been described to me as an "intermittent problem" because they're seasonal and we don't see large ones happening every year.

If they happened every year, it would become an obvious priority.

Preventing and tackling them both cost money and there are obvious questions around striking the balance between spending on both, not to mention wider affordability.

But climate change is predicted to bring more long, dry spells which create the tinderbox of summer 2026 and so all of this may be seen as an investment in the future.

For five weeks, land managers with very opposing views on how the uplands should be managed stood side by side battling the enormous blaze which was sweeping through the Cairngorms.

They found a common purpose and it's hoped that now seeing the countryside through a prism of wildfire risk may now be the unifier which sees them exchanging at least some practices - even if their end goals for the landscape still differ wildly.

articles.title: I was in so much pain I could barely feed my cats - now I'm back as a pro wrestler
articles.summary: The AEW star Jamie Hayter is set for two big shows in Glasgow and at Wembley Stadium in London this week.
articles.body:
Professional wrestling storylines are often built around surprise moments, from unexpected returns to sudden plot twists.

However when British star Jamie Hayter suffered two herniated discs in her back in 2023, she feared she would never get back in the ring.

It left her in constant pain, barely able to feed her cats - and wondering if her career was over.

But the grappler, who competes with All Elite Wrestling, told BBC News that the experience gave her a better perspective on her wrestling.

And the 31-year-old from Southampton is back on home turf this week, performing in two shows at Glasgow's OVO Hydro arena and then at AEW's biggest event of the year, called All In and held at Wembley Stadium on Sunday.

Her injury left her out of action for a year.

"The worst was the first few months because I was really unsure of things," she said.

"The pain was at its highest and I was bed bound – the most I could do was get up, feed my cats, make a coffee and then wobble back to bed.

"I was sitting there depressed, think I'm not doing anything, nothing is going on in my life, and it was hard to see a positive light. Weeks felt like they were taking years to go by.

"It helped me come back with a better mentality for wrestling than I had before, just more mellowed out and with a better understanding of what is worth getting upset over."

Hayter and her tag team partner, fellow Brit Alex Windsor, are in one of Sunday's featured bouts, challenging for the promotion's women's tag team titles in front of more than 40,000 people.

It comes about a decade after Hayter learned she had ADHD. She says her career of bumps and bruises is helping her cope with the diagnosis.

"It was not a surprise because my family are all neurodivergent and my siblings have autism," she recalls.

"At school someone would say 'oh, you might have ADHD' but it never went beyond that, other than getting a little extra help for exams which I always really struggled with.

"It was a relief being diagnosed at the end of the day. It meant I can understand my brain a little better, and how I process and work with things."

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

The wrestler, real name Paige Woodling, says she can still find things overwhelming a lot of the time.

Being in the ring, though, has proved to be a help over the years, letting her "focus on one thing".

"I need to be in the zone with it, and I wish my brain could do that with other things too. But I think it mixes a lot of things together – there's an audience I want to entertain, it's my job, there are consequences if you don't do it well and I never want to let down the people who are there."

Given Hayter is regarded as one of the top wrestlers in AEW - the world's second biggest promotion behind industry giant World Wrestling Entertainment - it might seem unlikely that she would let down people.

Away from the squared circle though, and she admits things can be harder when the spotlights are off.

"You hear people say 'oh, being neurodivergent is my super power' and I hate that, because it's a debilitating thing. It can be a lot to deal with, and at points I do slip – I'll get overwhelmed with having places to be, or things to do, and life things go out the window.

"I'm still learning to manage it all better."

Hayter first fell in love with the industry when young, watching online clips and videos of matches, with brash anti-hero Stone Cold Steve Austin - a beer drinking, brawling and swearing star of the late 90s and early 2000s - an early inspiration.

"Nothing has ever captured me like wrestling did, not movies or TV or music," she says.

"Wrestling had this weird trance on me. I wanted to watch more, understand it and eventually do it, and I decided I was going to be a wrestler or a stuntwoman."

A prolific career on the British wrestling scene followed, which led to a stint in Japan, and a blink-and-you'll -miss-it appearance on WWE's development show NXT, where she lost to Scottish wrestler Piper Niven in Glasgow.

That was one of very few Scottish appearances for Hayter, who says she's eager to sample a "proper Glasgow crowd" at the Hydro, as AEW record their flagship TV shows Dynamite and Collision in the city.

She has been with the company since 2021, becoming a fixture of their women's division and winning the women's singles title on one occasion .

Earlier this year she was paired up with Norwich native Alex Windsor to form a team calling the Brawling Birds - a fan favourite duo fond of both brawls and booze.

"It's pretty close to us in real life, " she laughs.

"We're pretty tomboyish, we don't take things too seriously and we both like going to the pub. We're loud and boisterous but in a good way, and then you crank that up to 10 – we do ham it up a bit for an American audience."

After recovering from her debilitating injury, Hayter is now in far more optimistic spirits, chatting in the bar of a Glasgow hotel.

She jokes her onscreen character has varied inspirations from Farrah Fawcett in Charlie's Angels to Daphne in Scooby Doo, and this week's shows promise to be some of the biggest in her life.

Hayter also feels AEW itself could feature more women's wrestling - the promotion has yet to headline a major supercard with a women's match in its existence.

"Women in wrestling have proven themselves - we can do great matches, good promos and make you want to see a match.

"There's some inherent misogyny in wrestling as a whole, and women wrestlers for years would always get common tropes.

"But there are lots of different flavours of women's wrestling, and we can tap into that more."

Hayter herself says she's ready for any of those flavours, whatever comes next.

"I think I'm someone that just rolls with the punches. Whatever comes next I'll go full force with it."

articles.title: Yamaha Awards Over $225,000 in Q2 2026 Access Grants
articles.summary: Let's get the kids back outside!
articles.body:
Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative Awards Over $225,000 in Q2 2026 Grants

Funding Supports Youth Outdoor Education, Trail Stewardship, and Responsible Motorized Recreation

MARIETTA, Ga. – August 25, 2026 – Yamaha Motor Corp., USA, awarded more than $225,000 in second-quarter funding through the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative (Yamaha OAI), supporting seven organizations working to expand responsible access to outdoor and motorized recreation through youth education, trail stewardship, ride area safety improvements, and enhanced access opportunities.

The latest grants fund projects ranging from youth boating, fishing, and bicycling education to trail rehabilitation, new trail development, improved wayfinding, and track and riding-area safety. The quarter also brings together Yamaha OAI and Yamaha Rightwaters to help expand outdoor recreation opportunities for young people through boating and fishing programs on California's Catalina Island.

"This quarter's recipients demonstrate the many ways responsible recreation and long-term outdoor access go hand-in-hand, from introducing young people to lifelong outdoor activities to maintaining the trails and riding areas enthusiasts depend on," said Steve Nessl, Yamaha Motorsports marketing director. "We're also proud to continue our support of All Kids Bike for a fifth year, helping give kindergarteners at more than 50 elementary schools nationwide the opportunity to learn how to ride a bike through their physical education programs."

Q2 2026 Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative Grant Recipients

Yamaha OAI awarded grants to the following organizations during the second-quarter funding cycle:

Catalina Outdoor Adventure Club (RJ Nautical, Avalon, Calif.) received funding, along with a 40-horsepower outboard motor contributed by Yamaha Rightwaters, to expand youth boating and fishing programs on Catalina Island.

GARTRA – Georgia Recreational Trail Riders Association (Nelson Powersports, Blue Ridge, Ga.) received funding to support trail maintenance at seven OHV areas throughout Georgia.

Quad Cities ATV Club (Five Seasons Sports, Eveleth, Minn.) will rehabilitate two heavily used trails that connect riders to a regional trail system in northern Minnesota.

San Luis Valley Great Outdoors (Peak Motor Sports, Alamosa, Colo.) will develop a new connector trail and improve wayfinding signage in Colorado's San Luis Valley.

Strider Education Foundation / All Kids Bike will expand its Kindergarten PE Learn-to-Ride Program to 12 additional schools nationwide, continuing a partnership with Yamaha OAI that began in 2021.

Summit County Off-Road Riders (SCORR) (Silverthorne Powersports, Silverthorne, Colo.) will make track maintenance and safety improvements at its motocross facility in Dillon, Colorado.

West Central Montana Avalanche Foundation (Five Valley Honda Yamaha, Missoula, Mont.) will support backcountry trail maintenance and safety education for motorized recreation in the Seeley Lake region.

Yamaha OAI accepts applications year-round and awards grants quarterly to eligible organizations working to improve access to outdoor recreation. The program prioritizes projects that promote safe and responsible motorized recreation, maintain and improve trails and riding areas, and help protect sustainable access to public lands.

The application deadline for Q3 2026 grants is September 30, 2026. Public land managers, riding clubs, land stewardship organizations, and outdoor recreation groups are encouraged to learn more and apply at YamahaOAI.com.

Follow Yamaha Outdoors on social media at @YamahaOutdoors and share your adventures using #Yamaha, #YamahaOAI, #REALizeYourAdventure, and #ProvenOffRoad.

About the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative

Since 2008, the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative has led the powersports industry in supporting responsible access to our nation's public lands for outdoor enthusiasts. With more than $8 million contributed to over 575 projects across the country, Yamaha has directly and indirectly supported thousands of miles of motorized recreation trails, maintained and rehabilitated riding and hunting areas, improved staging areas, supplied organizations with essential OHV safety education, built bridges over fish-bearing streams, helped children learn to ride bicycles, and partnered with local outdoor enthusiast communities to improve access to public lands. Each quarter, Yamaha accepts applications from nonprofit or tax-exempt organizations, including OHV riding and cycling clubs and associations, national, state, and local public land-use agencies, outdoor enthusiast associations, and land conservation groups with an interest in protecting, improving, expanding, and/or maintaining access for safe, responsible, and sustainable public use.

For updated guidelines, the application form, and the latest Outdoor Access Initiative news, please visit YamahaOAI.com. If you have specific inquiries about the Yamaha Outdoor Access Initiative, you can reach the dedicated hotline at 1-877-OHV-TRAIL (877-648-8724), email OHVAccess@Yamaha-Motor.com, or send correspondence to:

articles.title: ‘It’s all about her and only her’: Criticism mounts for Angel Reese after ‘selfish’ play

articles.body:
Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream are in the midst of a four-game winning streak, and on Monday night, in a win over the Los Angeles Sparks , Reese etched her name in the history books. Reese snagged a record-breaking 26 rebounds in the game, the most dominant performance on the glass in the WNBA's 30-year history.

Reese also recorded yet another double-double, scoring 11 points in the contest. However, the manner in which she scored her final bucket has been deemed "unethical" by some fans.

With the outcome already decided and less than 20 seconds remaining in regulation, Reese was camped out back at the Dream's basket rather than running back to defend with her teammates, which left her wide open to collect an outlet pass and reach double-digit scoring.

"We all know Angel Reese just wants her double double and look how she gets it. Cherry picking per usual. If she doesn't get to the free throw line or cherry pick, she can't score. It's all about her and only her," posted one person on X who wan't a fan of her tactics.

We all know Angel Reese just wants her double double and look how she gets it. Cherry picking per usual. If she doesn’t get to the free throw line or cherry pick, she can’t score. It’s all about her and only her. pic.twitter.com/DS0WlKPD8u — HeHateMe (@_HeHateMee_) August 25, 2026

We all know Angel Reese just wants her double double and look how she gets it.

Cherry picking per usual. If she doesn’t get to the free throw line or cherry pick, she can’t score. It’s all about her and only her. pic.twitter.com/DS0WlKPD8u

— HeHateMe (@_HeHateMee_) August 25, 2026

The original poster wasn't alone in his criticisms of Reese.

"Even half the time she does this she blows the layup and can't score. Shoots under 50% from within a couple ft of the basket. How's that even possible? Great rebounder but she's absolutely unskilled," one fan posted on X.

"Ahhh, now I can plainly see why she misses these layups. She jumps with both feet at the same time. Why hasn't this been corrected?" another fan wondered.

"What a low IQ and selfish play. Up 7 with 15 seconds left and she doesn't run the clock out?" someone else posted.

There's no denying that Reese's offensive game needs some polishing, but even so, her impact is undeniable. Reese is on a surefire path to ending up in the Hall of Fame, and with the Dream peaking right before the playoffs, she might even beat her rival Caitlin Clark to a WNBA championship.

articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he does not support a planned event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat at Madison Square Garden,.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has said he does not support a planned event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat at Madison Square Garden, while noting that the city may not have the legal authority to stop the private gathering.Bhagwat is scheduled to address around 5,000 members of the Indian diaspora at the iconic New York venue on August 29. His visit to the United States is part of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's centenary-year global outreach programme."I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,â Mamdani said at a news conference on Tuesday.Mamdani was responding to questions about the RSS, the proposed event and protests against Bhagwat's appearance. He was also asked whether the gathering should be cancelled.The mayor, who is the first Indian-American to hold the post in New York City, said his views were influenced partly by his family background.âI also stand here as the first Indian-American Mayor in our city's history, and my mother's family is all still in India," Mamdani said.He said his understanding of India was based on the idea of a society where people of different backgrounds could belong equally.He said the vision of India that he was taught by his family and the one that he grew up being very familiar with was that of "a pluralistic society, of a secular republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India".Mamdani said he was opposed to what he described as an increasingly exclusionary political movement.âAnd it has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision of any country, frankly, and so it is one that I find myself in deep opposition to, not only as an Indian-American but also as the Mayor of a city that believes deeply in the belonging of each and every person, no matter their colour, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from,â Mamdani said.Protests planned over Bhagwat eventThe planned appearance has faced opposition from several interfaith and civil rights organisations. Groups including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Centre of New York held a press conference outside New York City Hall and called for the event to be cancelled.Bhagwat arrived in the US on Tuesday as part of the RSS's centenary-year outreach. During his stay in New York, he is also expected to participate in the Universal Oneness programme.The event is being organised by AHEAD Forum, which said in a social media post that Bhagwat would attend the Universal Oneness Celebration in New York on August 29.âThe event carries a timeless and universal message: 'The world is one family'. It calls upon us to look beyond artificial divisions and differences, recognise the bonds that unite humanity, and embrace a spirit of mutual respect, harmony, and oneness,â the post said.Bhagwat's wider international tour includes the US, Canada and the UK as part of the Sangh's centenary-year global outreach programme.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: The Voice Lindsay Clancy Says Told Her to Kill Lasted Just 18 Minutes. A Psychologist Says That’s ‘Very, Very Unusual’
articles.summary: Clancy is charged with the murders of her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan
articles.body:
Lindsay Clancy is accused of intentionally killing her three young children

Her defense attorney has argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis

A forensic psychologist testified that Clancy said a male voice told her, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself"

A psychologist testified that Lindsay Clancy reported hearing a male voice for the first and only time during the roughly 18 minutes the killings of her three children occurred.

"She only experienced it for the 18 minutes or so that it took to kill the children," Kirk Heilbrun, who evaluated the mother of three, testified on Monday, August 24, the Boston Globe reported. "And to put it mildly, that would be a very, very unusual pattern or manifestation of how this kind of thing comes about."

Heilbrun told the court that Clancy said the male voice told her, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the kids so you can kill yourself."

Heilbrun said the timing was unusual and said it could be a way to lessen her culpability.

Prosecutors allege Clancy deliberately strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan — with exercise bands at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023.

After killing the children, she jumped out of a second-story window in an apparent suicide attempt, leaving her paralyzed.

Clancy, 36, does not deny she killed her children.

Her defense attorney has argued that she was not criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the murders.

Heilbrun also testified that Clancy killed her children because she thought the children would suffer without her and that killing them would allow them to be "together in heaven."

During testimony on Tuesday, August 25, forensic psychiatrist Gregory Saathoff, testified that Clancy, who he interviewed twice in 2026, told him she first killed her son Dawson, then Cora and then her youngest child.

"All during this time where this voice is over and over, over again saying, "This is your last chance. You have to kill the children before you kill yourself," he testified.

Asked by a prosecutor if there was significance to the fact that the voice told her to kill the children, but did not tell her how to kill them, he responded, "Yes."

"You know, just like adults, children have a will to survive — a strong, strong will to survive. I think it's just part of being human," Saathoff said. "I mean, they are active. They can walk. They can run."

The closely watched four-week trial held in Plymouth County Superior Court has drawn national attention and sparked debate about postpartum mental health and the treatment of women experiencing psychiatric crises.

More than 70 witnesses have testified during the proceedings including medical experts, friends, law enforcement and Clancy's ex-husband Patrick.
